title: Alternating Sum of Triangular Reciprocals
description: The alternating sum of reciprocals of triangular numbers equals 4·ln(2) - 2: ∑(-1)^{n+1}·2/(n(n+1)) = 4·ln(2) - 2 ≈ 0.7726.

meta.author: Classical (formalized in Lean 4 with Mathlib)
meta.assumptions: Two axioms encode the alternating harmonic series (Mercator series at x=1). Proving these requires Abel's theorem for boundary convergence of power series, not yet in Mathlib.
originalContributions: Alternating triangular reciprocals = 4·ln(2) - 2 via partial fractions

overview.historicalContext: This identity extends the classical result $\sum 2/(n(n+1)) = 2$ (proved by Leibniz in 1673 via telescoping) to its alternating variant. The alternating harmonic series $\ln 2 = 1 - 1/2 + 1/3 - 1/4 + \cdots$ was first computed by Nicolaus Mercator in his 1668 work *Logarithmotechnia*, where he expanded $\ln(1+x) = x - x^2/2 + x^3/3 - \cdots$ and evaluated at $x=1$. This was one of the earliest known conditionally convergent series — its terms can be rearranged to converge to any real value (Riemann's rearrangement theorem, 1854). The boundary convergence at $x=1$ requires Abel's theorem on power series, proved by Abel in 1826. The alternating triangular reciprocal series combines both ideas: partial fractions reduce it to two instances of the Mercator series, yielding the transcendental value $4\ln 2 - 2$.
overview.proofStrategy: Use partial fractions: (-1)^{n+1}·2/(n(n+1)) = 2·(-1)^{n+1}/n - 2·(-1)^{n+1}/(n+1). This splits the series into the alternating harmonic series (= ln 2) and its shifted variant (= 1 - ln 2). Combining: 2·ln(2) - 2·(1 - ln(2)) = 4·ln(2) - 2.
keyInsights: Partial fractions split each alternating term into a difference of two simpler alternating terms, reducing a product-denominator series to known single-denominator series

The shifted alternating harmonic series ∑(-1)^{n+1}/(n+1) = 1 - ln(2) follows from the standard series by removing the first term and negating — a general technique for deriving shifted-index series identities

The result 4·ln(2) - 2 ≈ 0.7726 shows the alternating sum converges to a transcendental number, unlike the non-alternating case which equals exactly 2, illustrating how sign alternation introduces logarithmic values
The two axioms (alternating harmonic series = ln 2) encode Abel's theorem for boundary convergence of power series — a key gap in Mathlib that blocks many series identities
The proof's use of HasSum.mul_left and HasSum.sub demonstrates Mathlib's algebraic API for infinite sums: series can be scaled and subtracted like finite sums when convergence is established

sections.title: Header and Imports
sections.summary: Module docstring describing the proof strategy (partial fractions decomposition into Mercator series), the two axioms required (Abel's theorem gap), and the connection to the non-alternating triangular reciprocals proof. Opens Finset, BigOperators, Filter, Topology, and Real.

sections.title: Alternating Harmonic Series (Axiomatized)
sections.summary: Two axioms encoding the Mercator series at x=1: the alternating harmonic series = ln(2) and its shifted variant = 1 - ln(2). These require Abel's theorem for boundary convergence.

sections.title: Main Theorem
sections.summary: The core result: HasSum for ∑(-1)^{n+1}·2/(n(n+1)) = 4·ln(2) - 2. Proof via funext partial fractions, then combining two HasSum results with mul_left and sub.

sections.title: Unscaled Corollary
sections.summary: Derives ∑(-1)^{n+1}/(n(n+1)) = 2·ln(2) - 1 by dividing the main result by 2 using const_smul with 2⁻¹.

sections.title: Summability
sections.summary: The alternating series is summable, derived directly from the main HasSum result.

sections.title: Finite Partial Sums
sections.summary: Computes S₁ = 1, S₂ = 2/3, S₃ = 5/6, S₄ = 11/15 via norm_num, showing oscillation around the limit 4·ln(2) - 2.

crossReferences.description: Extends the non-alternating result ∑2/(n(n+1)) = 2 to its alternating variant. Both use partial fractions and telescoping ideas.
Both are classical infinite series with exact closed-form sums. The alternating geometric series ∑(-1)^n·r^n = 1/(1+r) and alternating triangular reciprocals both involve sign-alternating terms.

conclusion.summary: The alternating triangular reciprocal series identity is fully verified modulo two well-known axioms (the Mercator series). The proof cleanly decomposes the alternating product series into two standard alternating series using partial fractions.
conclusion.implications: This demonstrates that alternating figurate number reciprocals yield transcendental values (4·ln(2) - 2) even when the non-alternating counterpart (2) is rational. The technique generalizes: ∑(-1)^{n+1}/(n(n+k)) can be similarly decomposed into k shifted alternating harmonic series.
openQuestions: Prove the alternating harmonic series = ln(2) without axioms (requires Abel's theorem in Lean)
Formalize the connection to the digamma function: ∑(-1)^{n+1}/(n(n+1)) = 2·ψ(1) + 2·γ where γ is the Euler-Mascheroni constant
